interviewQuestions.question: What does "zero trust" actually mean, in one or two sentences you'd say to start an answer?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It means no request is trusted because of where it came from — every request gets its own identity, device, and context check, regardless of network location. "Never trust, always verify" is the slogan, but the substance is that network position stops being a proxy for trustworthiness.

That's a direct rejection of the older perimeter model, where getting past the firewall or connecting over VPN granted broad, largely unchecked access to everything inside. Zero trust instead asks, for every single request: is this specific identity, on this specific device, in this specific context, allowed to do this specific thing right now? That's a per-request, per-resource decision instead of a one-time, network-wide one.

It's worth being precise that it's an architectural stance built from several concrete pieces — strong identity (MFA), device posture checks, microsegmentation, and continuous (not just point-in-time) verification — rather than a single product you install. A vendor selling "a zero trust box" that still grants broad access after one login hasn't actually implemented the model, just renamed the old one.

**Testing:** whether you can define it precisely — the specific assumption it rejects — rather than reciting the marketing phrase.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How does microsegmentation under zero trust differ from the network segmentation covered earlier in this group, and why does the difference matter for containing a breach?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Traditional segmentation — VLANs, subnets, firewall rules between zones — still groups many hosts together, and once you're inside a zone, reachability within it is often wide open. It's a real improvement over a fully flat network, but the blast radius of a compromised host is still "everything in this zone," which can be dozens or hundreds of systems.

Microsegmentation pushes the boundary down to the individual workload. Instead of "this subnet can reach that subnet," the policy says "the checkout service can reach exactly the payments API on port 443, and nothing else" — enforced through software-defined policy (a service mesh, cloud security groups, host agents) rather than physical network topology. A compromised checkout service, under that policy, literally cannot open a connection to the user database or an internal admin panel, even if they happen to run on the same physical hardware.

The containment difference is significant in practice: a breach that would have spread to a whole zone under coarse segmentation gets stopped at the single compromised workload under microsegmentation, because the network itself refuses the lateral connection rather than relying on the attacker not trying it. The cost is that every legitimate dependency has to be explicitly mapped and allowed — undocumented dependencies break loudly the moment default-deny is turned on, which is why rollouts do this incrementally, starting with the highest-value services.

**Testing:** whether you can name the specific mechanism that shrinks blast radius, not just that microsegmentation 'sounds more secure.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design

interviewQuestions.question: A leadership team wants to move to zero trust but expects it to be a single infrastructure purchase completed in a quarter. How would you correct that expectation and describe a realistic rollout?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by separating the product from the architecture: buying a gateway labeled "zero trust" doesn't get you the property unless the underlying trust decisions actually changed — a lot of vendor tooling still grants broad access after one check, just with new branding. So the real work isn't a purchase, it's changing how access decisions get made across identity, devices, and network policy, and that touches nearly every system, which is why it can't land in a quarter.

A realistic sequence: first, strong identity everywhere — MFA, retiring password-only auth — because every later step depends on trustworthy identity signals; this alone is months of work across every app and SSO integration. Next, device posture checks on the highest-value resources, not the whole estate at once. Then microsegmentation starting with the most critical services, where the payoff justifies the effort of mapping real dependencies. Only after that do you start shrinking the old VPN's broad grants — and even then, the VPN often survives as a fallback for legacy systems that can't yet talk to the new policy engine.

I'd frame this to leadership as a multi-quarter, risk-prioritized program with measurable milestones per phase (percentage of users on MFA, percentage of critical services microsegmented), not a single deliverable — and I'd flag upfront that skipping straight to buying a product without this sequencing tends to produce exactly the rebranded-VPN outcome that gives zero trust a bad reputation internally.

**Testing:** whether you can push back on an unrealistic scope with a credible, staged alternative — a real staff-level communication skill, not just technical knowledge.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Rollout

interviewQuestions.question: What's a legitimate criticism of zero trust that you'd bring up yourself, rather than waiting to be asked?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
That it doesn't remove single points of failure, it relocates them — and if that relocation isn't taken seriously, you've traded one weak point for another without actually reducing risk. The VPN gateway used to be the thing whose compromise granted broad access; under zero trust, that role shifts to the identity provider and the policy engine. Compromise the identity provider, and an attacker can potentially mint valid-looking credentials for the exact continuous checks the whole architecture relies on — which is arguably a scarier failure mode than a compromised VPN box, because it undermines the trust signal itself rather than just one path into the network.

The second honest cost is operational: continuous per-request checks add latency, and microsegmentation adds a real, ongoing maintenance burden — every legitimate service dependency has to be known and kept current, and dependency drift causes real outages when a team adds a new call path and forgets to update the policy. It also adds friction for end users who are used to connecting once and working all day, and rolling that out without change management produces real pushback that can stall or reverse a migration.

So the honest pitch isn't "zero trust has no downside," it's "the trade of latency and operational overhead for a much smaller blast radius and no single perimeter chokepoint is usually worth it for high-value systems" — while investing real effort in hardening the identity provider and policy engine that the whole model now depends on.

**Testing:** whether you can critique your own preferred architecture credibly, which reads as more senior than defending it uncritically.
